extracted.intended_audience: analysts in Federal agencies preparing regulatory analyses and supporting documentation for rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing regulatory analysis (benefit-cost and cost-effectiveness) and required supporting materials for Federal rulemakings, including identification of the need for action, alternatives, and quantification/monetization, plus statutory analytic supplements (RFA, Unfunded Mandates, NEPA, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for Federal Regulatory Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recommending Federal regulatory action, an agency must demonstrate that the proposed action is necessary and identify the problem the agency intends to address (including market failures or other compelling public needs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe statutory or judicial authority, the extent of discretion, and regulatory instruments considered. Explain whether the action addresses a significant market failure (externality, market power, inadequate/asymmetric information) or another social purpose (improving government functioning, distributional fairness, privacy). Present qualitative and, where feasible, quantitative description of the problem and show that government intervention is likely to do more good than harm. Consider whether State/local action or non-regulatory alternatives (antitrust, litigation, compensation systems) are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Elements of a Regulatory Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A good regulatory analysis should include (1) a statement of the need for the proposed action, (2) an examination of alternative approaches, and (3) an evaluation of the benefits and costs—quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and the main alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explanation of how actions link to expected benefits, identification of baseline(s), side-effects and ancillary benefits, quantification/monetization where possible, and discussion of important non-quantified effects. Provide a summary of benefit and cost estimates for each alternative including qualitative and non-monetized factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain Linkage Between Rule Requirements and Expected Benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the actions required by the rule are linked to the expected benefits (e.g., indicate how additional safety equipment will reduce safety risks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform this analysis for each alternative. Make causal/mechanistic linkages clear so a third party can see how estimates and conclusions were reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify a Baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits and costs must be defined in comparison with a clearly stated baseline (normally a 'no action' baseline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons to a 'next best' alternative are also useful. State what the world will be like absent the proposed rule and use that baseline consistently across alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify Expected Side-Effects and Ancillary Benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify undesirable side-effects and ancillary benefits of the proposed regulatory action and alternatives, and include them with direct benefits and costs as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider indirect, displaced, or ancillary effects and incorporate them in quantitative estimates when feasible; otherwise describe them qualitatively and note their importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify and Monetize Benefits and Costs Where Feasible; Discuss Non-Quantified Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop quantitative estimates and convert them to dollar amounts if possible; where not possible, provide qualitative description and, if important, threshold/break-even analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When important benefits/costs cannot be monetized, use professional judgment to assess their importance, indicate which non-quantified effects are most important, and carry out threshold analysis to show how large or small unquantified values would have to be to change conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Benefit-Cost Analysis (BCA) to Identify Efficient Alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: When all benefits and costs can be expressed in monetary units, use BCA to identify the alternative that generates the largest net benefits to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report incremental benefits and costs; choose alternatives that maximize net benefits. Do not rely on benefit-cost ratios alone — the ratio is not a meaningful indicator of net benefits and can be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA) Where Appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use CEA for major rulemakings whose primary benefits are improved public health and safety (when a valid effectiveness measure exists), and for other cases where monetization of all benefits is infeasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare CEA for all major public health and safety rulemakings where valid effectiveness measures can be developed. Also perform BCA when monetary values can be assigned; if some primary benefits cannot be monetized, present CEA and BCA as feasible and explain limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose Appropriate Effectiveness Metrics for Health and Safety (e.g., lives saved, QALYs, ELs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select one or more measures of effectiveness (lives saved, life-years saved, equivalent lives, QALYs) that permit comparison of regulatory alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer final outcomes (lives, life-years) over intermediate outputs. Consider integrated measures when morbidity and mortality both matter. Explain choice of measures, consider fairness (use population averages for life expectancy adjustments), and report multiple measures when useful. OMB does not require a specific effectiveness measure but encourages reporting with multiple measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Incremental Analysis Over Averages
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing alternatives, prefer incremental cost-effectiveness and incremental net benefits rather than average cost-effectiveness or benefit-cost ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Average ratios can be misleading; incremental comparisons reveal dominance relationships and avoid mistaken choices. Eliminate inferior alternatives by principles of strong and weak dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct Cost and Effectiveness Measures Carefully in CEA
rubrics_metrics.description: Include all relevant societal costs (public and private), avoid double-counting, and use net costs (gross cost minus cost savings) in the numerator; select effectiveness measures that reflect final outcomes or appropriately weighted outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing gross costs by a monetary value on life extension if life-years are used in denominator. Explain choice of effectiveness metric and, where quality/heterogeneity exists (e.g., wetlands), ensure the measure captures variability in value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and Documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good analysis is transparent: state assumptions, time horizon, discount rates, provide sensitivity analyses, cite all data sources, and include appendices documenting models and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure a qualified third party can see how estimates and conclusions were arrived at. Provide an executive summary and a standardized accounting statement. Include references, model documentation, and results of formal uncertainty analyses as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct Sensitivity Analysis and Report Switch Points
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide sensitivity analysis to reveal whether results are sensitive to plausible changes in assumptions and inputs and identify 'switch points' where conclusions change sign or ranking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary one variable at a time or combinations of variables; where outcomes change (positive to negative net benefits or ranking changes), further analysis is required. Use sensitivity analysis to show robustness and to prioritize where better information is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Risk and Uncertainty: Provide Expected Values and Distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide expected-value estimates and, where available, distributions around estimates; when only bounds are available, present 95% and 5% confidence bounds if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize summary statistics easy to understand, assume risk neutrality unless otherwise justified (and explain departures). Make full disclosure about uncertainty and show alternative plausible assumptions when uncertainty is consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal Probabilistic Analysis for Very Large Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply formal probabilistic analysis (simulation, expert elicitation) for complex rules with multiple large uncertainties and required for rules with annual effects exceeding $1 billion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Delphi or expert elicitation to quantify parameter distributions, combine via Monte Carlo simulations, pay attention to correlated inputs (do not assume independence by default), and present probabilistic results clearly in graphs/tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Professional Judgment; No One-Size-Fits-All Formula
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality analysis requires competent professional judgment; different regulations will call for different emphases depending on complexity and sensitivity to assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should balance thoroughness with practical limits, exercise judgement about which alternatives to analyze in depth, and explain analytic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption Against Certain Types of Economic Regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption against some regulatory actions absent a demanding burden of proof: price controls in competitive markets; production/sales quotas in competitive markets; mandatory uniform quality standards when voluntary standards or disclosure suffice; and controls on entry into employment/production except in narrow cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid regulations that increase market power. Exceptions exist for health/safety entry controls (e.g., FAA tests) or management of common property resources (fisheries, airwaves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider a Range of Alternative Regulatory Approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: After determining that Federal regulation is appropriate, consider and analyze a manageable set of alternatives that modify attributes of the regulation (statutory choices, timing, enforcement, stringency, coverage, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate some alternatives through preliminary analysis but explore modifications to attributes (e.g., alternative statutory-compliant standards) and consider trade-offs between thoroughness and capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Choices Defined by Statute
rubrics_metrics.description: When statute establishes specific requirements and agency considers a more stringent standard, examine benefits and costs of reasonable alternatives reflecting statutory discretion including the specific statutory requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze alternatives within the scope of statutory language and agency discretion and include statutory minima/requirements as alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Compliance Dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how the timing of compliance affects net benefits; examine alternative compliance dates and lead times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delaying implementation can change benefits and costs (e.g., lost future benefits or production planning costs). Provide options with sufficient lead time where warranted to reduce overall costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Enforcement Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider alternative monitoring and enforcement frameworks (on-site inspections, periodic reporting, structured penalties, random or parametric monitoring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify enforcement frameworks that provide appropriate incentives at least cost; when monitoring methods differ in costs and effectiveness, choose the most appropriate approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Degrees of Stringency
rubrics_metrics.description: Study multiple levels of regulatory stringency to understand how benefits and costs and their distribution vary with stringency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize marginal costs generally rise with stringency while marginal benefits may decline; use incremental analysis to compare levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Requirements for Different Sized Firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider setting different requirements for large and small firms based on estimated differences in expected compliance costs or benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for fixed costs of compliance that disproportionately affect small firms. If the rule significantly impacts many small entities, follow Regulatory Flexibility Act requirements and consult SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Requirements for Different Geographic Regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where benefits and costs vary substantially across regions, consider geographically differentiated requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine regional disparities and consider whether regional rules, variances, or federal harmonization are more efficient; evaluate potential costs of fragmented State/local regulation versus national uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance Standards Rather Than Design Standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer performance standards (outcome-based) over design standards (specifying means) because they give regulated parties flexibility to achieve objectives cost-effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh cost savings from flexibility against costs of monitoring and ensuring compliance; consider whether performance standards could create unacceptable local outcomes (hot spots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-Oriented Approaches Rather Than Direct Controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore market-oriented alternatives (fees, penalties, subsidies, tradable permits/offsets, bonds, insurance requirements, liability changes) that use economic incentives instead of command-and-control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider averaging, banking, and trading (ABT) programs where cost heterogeneity exists; ensure ABT does not create unacceptable local pollution concentrations. Evaluate cost reductions and potential distributional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informational Measures Rather Than Regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: When failures stem from inadequate or asymmetric information, consider informational remedies (standardized testing/rating, mandatory disclosure, government provision of information) before mandatory product standards or bans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate informational measures' benefits and costs, including costs of gathering/communicating information, displacement of other information, misinterpretation, and incentives to overinvest in disclosed characteristics. Prefer least intrusive measures sufficient to accomplish objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Double-Counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid counting the same change in social welfare more than once when listing and aggregating benefits and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with multiple ways to express the same welfare change and use categories that prevent overlap. State transfers separately to prevent misclassification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting Statement and Standardized Reporting Categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accounting statement with tables reporting benefit and cost estimates for each major rule, using mutually exclusive categories: monetized benefits/costs, quantified but not monetized, and qualitative (unquantified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report annualized estimates, primary/minimum/maximum estimates, source citations, and separate transfer reporting. Use suggested formats (table structure provided) and avoid double-counting across categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Benefits and Costs Over Time; Discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Present undiscounted streams of benefits and costs for each year of the analytic time horizon and annualized values using real discount rates of 3% and 7%, reporting monetized effects in 2001 dollars (convert with GDP deflator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin streams in the year rules begin to have effects, even if not effective immediately. Provide both undiscounted and annualized streams and disclose conversion methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and Rounding Conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported estimates should reflect feasible precision; choose rounding consistent with magnitude (e.g., $220 million rounded to nearest $10 million implies precision +/- $5 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate rounding levels to communicate implied precision. Provide enough precision to be meaningful and consistent with data quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate Reporting of Transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Report transfers separately and do not classify transfer payments as benefits or costs when they do not reflect net welfare changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate transfers caused by Federal budget actions ('on budget') from transfers between non-governmental parties ('off-budget'). If transfers have efficiency effects in addition to distributional effects, report those effects as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report Effects on State, Local, and Tribal Governments, Small Businesses, Wages, and Economic Growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify portions of benefits, costs, and transfers received by state/local/tribal governments, and, to the extent feasible, effects on small businesses, wages, and economic growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that rules costing less than $1 billion annually are likely to have minimal effects on economic growth. Use as many categories as necessary to describe redistributive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (RFA) for Small Entities
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rule may have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities, prepare a proposed and final regulatory flexibility analysis (RFA) under the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post RFAs online for public review where appropriate. Consult agency guidance and SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy. Follow SBREFA requirements (pre-proposal consultation) where applicable (e.g., EPA and OSHA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For rules that may result in aggregate expenditures of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted) by state/local/tribal governments or the private sector in any one year, prepare a written statement about benefits and costs under the Unfunded Mandates Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical requirements under Executive Order 12866 are similar; the same analysis may meet both requirements. Ensure compliance with statutory thresholds and documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the rule creates new information collection, paperwork, or recordkeeping burdens; OMB approval is required for new collections affecting 10 or more persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify the practical utility of the information for rule implementation and obtain an OMB control number for covered paperwork. Consult agency CIO for compliance assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Quality Guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure data and analysis meet agency and OMB information quality standards for information disseminated in support of proposed and final rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow government-wide guidelines and agency-specific rules; consult agency CIO and OMB's Statistical and Science Policy Branch for assistance. Maintain minimum quality standards defined by the Circular.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) Compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider environmental impacts per NEPA; prepare an environmental impact statement where a major Federal action significantly affects the quality of the human environment before issuing a final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete NEPA documentation in accordance with CEQ regulations (40 C.F.R. 1500-1508) and guidance; integrate NEPA analyses with rulemaking when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Impacts on Children (EO 13045)
rubrics_metrics.description: For economically significant rules concerning environmental health or safety risks that may disproportionately affect children, provide an evaluation of effects on children and explain why the planned regulation is preferable to other feasible alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address disproportionate risks to children to the extent permitted by law and consistent with agency mission; include evaluations in agency submissions to OMB/OIRA where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy Effects Statement (EO 13211)
rubrics_metrics.description: For significant energy actions, prepare and submit to OMB a Statement of Energy Effects describing any adverse effects on energy supply, distribution, or use and publish the statement or summary in the NPRM and final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow OMB Memorandum 01-27 for implementing EO 13211. Evaluate shortfalls in supply, price increases, and increased foreign energy use for the action and reasonable alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in Reporting Uncertainty (Confidence Bounds and Distributions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where only upper and lower bounds are provided, use 95% and 5% bounds if possible; when distributions exist, report them to aid public understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While detailed reporting of distributions is not mandatory, expected-value estimates and plausible bounds should be available upon request and included where informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Values of Uncertain Outcomes and Risk Preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there are probability distributions of outcomes or values, combine distributions to provide estimated benefits and costs and emphasize summary statistics consistent with assumed risk preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume risk neutrality in general; if adopting a different assumption, explain reasons. Use expected values (means) unless justified otherwise, and show sensitivity to risk preference assumptions when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative Assumptions and Hidden Assumptions Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Make key assumptions explicit, carry out sensitivity analyses using plausible alternative assumptions, and analyze estimation methods to reveal hidden assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If net benefits or rankings change under plausible alternative assumptions, conduct further analysis to determine appropriate assumptions and describe the rationale for chosen approaches.
